articles.title: Thoracic limb myology of Smutsia temminckii (Temminck's pangolin).
articles.authors: Christine Steyn, John Thomson Soley, Martina Rachel Crole
articles.abstract: The myrmecophagous Smutsia temminckii (Temminck's pangolin) is one of eight pangolin species, of threatened status worldwide and the only species present in southern Africa. S. temminckii utilises a bipedal gait for locomotion and will roll into a ball when vulnerable. The thoracic limbs are predominantly used to assist in exposing prey by employing scratch-digging in superficial substrates and breaking open ant nests. This study describes the thoracic limb musculature and muscle maps in S. temminckii, as well as discusses the peculiar adaptations of the thoracic limb to its unique lifestyle. The thoracic limbs of five S. temminckii were donated after they succumbed to either natural causes, electrocution or confiscation from the illegal wildlife trade. All ethical clearances were received. The muscles of the thoracic limbs were dissected and described, after which the bones were cleaned and the areas of muscle attachment identified and described. The muscles were generally well-developed with fleshy bodies and short tendons. The extrinsic muscles of the thoracic limb, and in particular M. cutaneous trunci, were prominent. M. triceps brachii, M. pronator teres and M. flexor digitorum profundus displayed additional bellies and extensive attachments. Individual metacarpophalangeal and digital muscles were noted. Two muscles were specifically named: the fleshy M. anconeus medialis and the long M. omoradialis. The musculature of S. temminckii shows clear adaptations to protraction and retraction of the forelimb, extension of the elbow joint, pronation and supination of the antebrachium, and flexion of the carpus and digits, which is consistent with scratch-digging, instead of weight-bearing. Both protractors of the forelimb and the prominent cutaneous musculature are involved when S. temminckii rolls up into a sphere during its defence posture. The muscle maps generated during this study aid in understanding the various muscle functions, as well as providing valuable information for postulating muscles in extinct pangolin species. The study may also aid workers in the veterinary field when treating musculoskeletal conditions in injured pangolins.

articles.title: Human foetal cortical slice cultures: A translational platform for studying early neurodevelopment.
articles.authors: Faye McLeod, Anna Dimtsi, Michael A Savage et al.
articles.abstract: The developing human neocortex is characterised by complex and dynamic changes in cellular architecture, neuronal organisation and activity. We previously described how human foetal cortical organotypic slice cultures, prepared from ethically sourced tissue could be used to investigate these processes. Cultures can be maintained for weeks, exhibiting features of the normal developing brain that are not replicated in current organoid models. Such cultures allow the possibility for experimental manipulation, for instance testing the effects of genetic mutations. Here we extend the characterisation of our model. We report that these organotypic cultures preserve the laminar organisation of the developing cortical wall and show considerable diversity of neuronal morphology. Employing bulk mRNA hybridisation for 794 genes (a "human neuropathology" gene panel), we identified consistent patterns of evolving gene expression between 0 and 14 days in vitro (DIV) across different tissue samples taken at 16-18 post-conceptional weeks (pcw). To put this in the context of the normal developmental pattern, we compared our data set with previously acquired tissue RNAseq data collected between 7-17 pcw (https://www.hdbr.org/expression). This indicated that many gene expression changes in vitro followed prior developmental trajectories, but others diverged strongly, including upregulated genes associated with responses to stress, and downregulated genes associated with the vascular function. This latter effect may reflect the redundancy of vascular development in culture. Notably, various genes associated with pre- and post- synaptic function, including both glutamate and GABA receptors, continued to be expressed strongly. Consistent with this, we observed spontaneous neuronal network activity in the subplate (SP) using targeted expression of the genetically encoded Ca2+ indicator, GCaMPf6, to post-mitotic neurons. The frequency of neuronal Ca2+ transients increased when blockers of either GABAA receptors or gap junctions were applied. Conversely, activity was significantly reduced by glutamatergic receptor antagonists and abolished by voltage gated sodium channel blockade. Neuronal Ca2+ transients were triggered directly by focal application of glutamate in the SP and subventricular zone, whereas cortical plate neurons exhibited weaker responses. This was consistent with levels of immunoreactivity for glutamate receptor sub-units in these compartments. In conclusion, the organotypic cultures show functional synaptic networks, supported by continued expression of the relevant synaptic protein machinery. These data provide further validation of organotypic cultures as a model for investigating and manipulating the early prenatal development of human neocortex, a period that is otherwise difficult to study.

articles.title: A Bibliometric Analysis of Body Donation Research (2006-2025): Perspectives From Medical Education, Ethics, and Policy.
articles.authors: Antong Zhao, Wang Liao, Yehui Lv
articles.abstract: Body donation is fundamental to anatomical education and biomedical research. The field has expanded from technical dissection to include ethical, regulatory, and educational dimensions, yet a systematic bibliometric analysis of its evolution is lacking. This study maps the knowledge structure, collaboration patterns, and research frontiers of the English-language body donation literature (2006-2025), focusing on the interplay among anatomical education, cultural ethics, and institutional governance. Publications were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection on August 5, 2026; 419 English-language articles met the eligibility criteria. CiteSpace (v6.2.R3) and VOSviewer (v1.6.18) were used to analyze collaboration networks, cocitation structures, citation bursts, and keyword co-occurence. Annual output increased steadily across three phases. The retrieved literature is concentrated in a small number of countries and institutions, a pattern inseparable from the language and database boundaries of the corpus, and collaboration is denser within regions than between them. Keyword co-occurence produced five clusters, mapped onto three analytical domains: anatomical education, cultural ethics, and institutional governance, the last with no cluster of its own. Organ donation concepts are still frequently conflated with body donation, and research frontiers have shifted from gross anatomy pedagogy toward legal regulation and public willingness. Body donation research has evolved from a technique-driven paradigm into a multidisciplinary field integrating humanistic care, legal frameworks, and educational innovation. Remaining gaps include the uneven representation of world regions in the indexed literature and the conflation of body and organ donation; both constrain culturally adaptable governance and anatomical education.

articles.title: Cervical biomechanical responses to parachute opening shock: effects of shock magnitude and initial body orientation.
articles.authors: Shuanghui Cao, Siqi Deng, Qingbo Dou et al.
articles.abstract: Injuries associated with parachute opening shock (POS) are a major form of trauma related to parachuting and remain an important concern in aerospace medicine. A full human body finite element model of POS incorporating a three-point harness system was developed, and its global dynamic response was evaluated using data from a physical POS test conducted with a Hybrid Ⅲ dummy. The first head acceleration peaks of the simulated and experimental responses were similar in magnitude and time to peak. The effects of POS magnitude and initial body orientation on cervical kinematics, regional loading, and local tissue biomechanical responses were subsequently investigated. The results indicated that POS induced nonuniform segmental cervical flexion and distinct loading patterns across different cervical regions. Increasing the POS magnitude generally increased cervical loads, intervertebral differential flexion, and tensile strains in the posterior cervical ligaments, whereas peak stress in individual vertebrae showed segmental variations. Changes in initial body orientation substantially altered the loading patterns of the middle and lower cervical spine by modifying harness load distribution and trunk motion. This study establishes a human body finite element framework that incorporates harness load transfer to reveal how POS magnitude and initial body orientation redistribute cervical loading from global trunk motion to segmental deformation and local tissue responses.

articles.title: Lower extremity joint biomechanics from a single crossover drop task demonstrate superior predictive potential for secondary ACL injuries than drop vertical jump or single leg landing tasks.
articles.authors: Nathan D Schilaty, Kim D Barber Foss, April L McPherson et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Secondary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries remain a significant concern after return-to-sport (RTS) following ACL reconstruction (ACLR), with rates as high as 24%. Identifying biomechanical predictors of re-injury is critical for improving RTS protocols. PURPOSE: To compare the predictive potential of three common landing tasks [drop vertical jump (DVJ), single-leg landing (SLL), and single-leg crossover drop (SCD)] for secondary ACL injury risk in post-ACLR athletes. METHODS: A multicenter cohort of 150 athletes (age 13-30 years) that were cleared for RTS post-ACLR completed DVJ, SLL, and SCD tasks during 3D motion analysis; 144 athletes data met criteria for analysis. Peak kinematic and kinetic variables (n = 126) were analyzed using a penalized logistic regression with an elastic net penalty. Predictive models were evaluated via ROC curves, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. RESULTS: The SCD task demonstrated the strongest predictive performance for secondary ACL injury, with a validated positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.57, negative predictive value (NPV) of 0.96, sensitivity of 80.0%, specificity of 88.9%, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.933. The DVJ demonstrated moderate predictive performance (PPV=0.43, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=85.7%, AUC=0.843), while the SLL demonstrated the lowest performance (PPV=0.33, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=78.6%, AUC=0.736). CONCLUSION: Lower extremity biomechanics during SCD provide greater predictive performance for secondary ACL injury compared with the DVJ or SLL. The findings suggest that SCD captures biomechanical characteristics relevant to secondary ACL injury risk and may improve identification of athletes at elevated risk following ACL reconstruction. However, further validation and model simplification are needed before clinical implementation as a stand-alone screening tool.

articles.title: Temporal evolution of EEG band power at freezing of gait onset in Parkinson's disease.
articles.authors: Brenda Luciano de Sousa Silva, Núbia Ribeiro Conceição, Caroline Ribeiro de Souza et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Although EEG studies have implicated theta-, alpha-, and beta-band activity in freezing of gait (FoG) in Parkinson's disease (PD), most have relied on resting-state comparisons, task contrasts, or connectivity analyses rather than modeling band-power changes around FoG onset. This study investigated the temporal evolution of EEG spectral power around FoG onset during ecological walking. METHODS: We analyzed a multimodal dataset comprising 10 individuals with PD and FoG during ecological walking. Two hundred and four FoG episodes were analyzed. EEG was recorded from 25 scalp electrodes and time-locked to FoG onset. Relative spectral power was computed for theta, alpha, and beta bands. Channel-wise piecewise linear mixed-effects models evaluated pre-FoG trends, onset-related shifts, and post-onset slope changes. Multiple comparisons were controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR, q < 0.05). RESULTS: Theta power showed no significant pre-FoG trend but increased abruptly at FoG onset at F3 and Fz. Alpha power exhibited a progressive pre-FoG increase at FP1, F3, F8, Fz, and Cz, whereas no onset-related or post-onset alpha effects survived FDR correction. Beta power showed no significant temporal modulation after correction. These findings indicate temporal profiles, with alpha changes preceding FoG and theta changes emerging at onset. CONCLUSION: FoG onset during ecological walking is associated with dissociable low-frequency EEG dynamics. Frontal and midline alpha increases may characterize a pre-freezing state, whereas abrupt frontal theta increases are associated with the transition into FoG. These patterns represent candidate electrophysiological features that require prospective validation before predictive or biomarker applications can be established.

articles.title: Predicting Military Training Outcome: A Prospective Cohort Study of Supervised Statistical Learning Classification Methods in British Army Recruits.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Thomas J O'Leary, Alexander T Carswell, Sarah Jackson et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Investigate predictors of failure and injury during British Army basic training and test the performance of statistical learning models to predict these outcomes. METHODS: 968 male and 450 female recruits had demographics, lifestyle habits, mood, physical performance, body composition, micronutrient status, and bone metabolism measured at week 1 of training. Associations between predictors and training outcome (failure; lower limb overuse musculoskeletal injury) were assessed by logistic regression. Training outcome was predicted by logistic regression, elastic net, random forests, and gradient boosting. RESULTS: 66% of men and 76% of women passed with 20% and 34% developing an injury. For men, slower 2.4 km run time (odds ratio [OR]=1.004, p=0.011) and higher symptoms of depression (OR=1.173, p=0.001) were associated with higher risk of failing, and lower areal bone mineral density (OR=0.008, p=0.002), slower 2.4 km run time (OR=1.006, p=0.011), previous stress fracture (OR=3.267, p=0.002), lower parathyroid hormone (OR=0.783, p=0.009), and lower c-telopeptide cross-links of type I collagen (βCTX) (OR=0.255, p=0.041) were associated with higher risk of injury. For women, slower 2.4 km run time (OR=1.009, p=0.009) and higher total 25-hydroxyvitamin-D (OR=1.013, p=0.001) were associated with higher risk of failing, and slower 2.4 km run time (OR=1.007, p=0.009), higher alcohol intake (OR=1.006, p=0.017), and lower βCTX (OR=0.057, p=0.026) were associated with higher risk of injury. Training outcome was poorly predicted in men and women (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve≤0.68). All models had low sensitivity and high specificity, but application of an outcome-specific threshold determined using the Youden Index improved sensitivity. CONCLUSIONS: Interventions to improve military training outcome should address aerobic fitness prior to starting training. Prediction models may be useful in identifying some 'at-risk' recruits.

articles.title: Task Force 11: Additional Cardiac Conditions and Considerations in Competitive Athletes.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Jeffrey J Hsu, Aaron L Baggish, Katherine E Economy et al.
articles.abstract: The recently updated AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities provides a comprehensive framework for guiding clinicians in the evaluation and management of competitive athletes. Divided into 11 Task Forces, it covers a broad range of cardiovascular diseases and clinical scenarios. Task Force 11 was devoted to cardiac conditions and considerations in athletes not included in the other Task Forces. Here, we present the detailed rationale for the clinical considerations covered in this section of the Scientific Statement. These topics include hypertension, commotio cordis, pulmonary embolism, performance-enhancing drugs and supplements, exercise in extreme environments (specifically altitude and scuba diving), and pregnancy.

articles.title: Task Force 10: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Masters Athletes with Underlying Cardiovascular Disease.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Elizabeth H Dineen, Mats Bӧrjesson, Eugene H Chung et al.
articles.abstract: Masters athletes are individuals ≥35 yr of age who place a high premium on exercise training and competition. This document details important cardiovascular conditions, risk factors, and data-driven discussion, which serve as the rationale for Section X from the 2025 AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes Cardiovascular Abnormalities. Disease-specific risk stratification and shared decision-making are the cornerstones for Masters athletes when considering competitive sports participation. Coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, incidental myocardial fibrosis, aortic enlargement and aneurysms, and valvular heart disease are included in this Task Force document.

articles.title: Task Force 9: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Athletes with Cardiac Channelopathies.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Belinda Gray, Eugene H Chung, Susan Etheridge et al.
articles.abstract: Cardiac channelopathies, including long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, and short QT syndrome, are heterogeneous conditions, which can lead to varying risks in athletes depending on their symptoms, disease severity, genotype, and therapies initiated. Historically, athletes with these conditions were excluded from participation with blanket restrictions, despite an absence of data. More recently, a number of studies have provided more scientific evidence to guide decision making and have been incorporated into these guidelines for athletes with cardiac channelopathies. Many athletes with these conditions may be supported in their decision to return to play as part of a shared decision-making model when they have been assessed, risk stratified, and appropriately treated by a specialist with expertise in these conditions.

articles.title: Task Force 8: Care of Competitive Athletes with Arrhythmias and Sudden Cardiac Arrest: Clinical Considerations and Electrocardiogram Interpretations.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Douglas Darden, Eugene H Chung, Kimberly G Harmon et al.
articles.abstract: This document outlines recommendations for managing competitive athletes with arrhythmias and risks of sudden cardiac arrest, emphasizing individualized risk assessment, shared decision-making, and return-to-play protocols tailored to each athlete's cardiac profile and sport demands. It provides evaluation strategies for ventricular arrhythmias, implantable cardiac defibrillators, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern/syndrome, and syncope, alongside guidance for electrocardiogram interpretation in athletes. A key focus is placed on differentiating between low-risk and high-risk conditions, with recommendations for treatment strategies and ongoing monitoring to ensure athletes' safety.

articles.title: Task Force 7: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Competitive Athletes with Aortopathy or Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Timothy W Churchill, Alan C Braverman, Flavio D'Ascenzi et al.
articles.abstract: Aortic disease represents an uncommon but important cause of sudden death among young competitive athletes. Important etiologies of aortic dilation in this population include bicuspid aortic valve, heritable thoracic aortic disease, and tricuspid aortic valve with unexplained aortic dilation. This document outlines a structured approach to the evaluation of young athletes with aortic disease with an emphasis on precise measurement of aortic dimensions with regular surveillance, careful evaluation for underlying etiologies, and shared decision-making. For each condition, we delineate low, moderate, and high-risk phenotypes and provide tailored guidance regarding sport participation. Additionally, guidance for athletes with spontaneous coronary artery dissection is also reviewed.

articles.title: Task Force 6: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Competitive Athletes with Congenital Heart Disease.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Julie A Brothers, Peter N Dean, Silvana Molossi et al.
articles.abstract: Athletes with congenital heart disease are commonly restricted from competitive sports participation based on limited data regarding exercise-induced sudden cardiac death risk. For most athletes, the myriad of benefits derived from participating in competitive sports outweighs the risk. This document reviews the cardiac assessment that may be considered for children, adolescents, and young adults with congenital heart disease. By utilizing anatomy, physiology, symptoms, and cardiac testing, together with shared decision-making, the authors propose a strategy to help guide medical providers advising their patients on sports participation.

articles.title: Task Force 5: Clinical Considerations for Myocarditis and Selected Cardiovascular Conditions, Including Valvular Heart Disease.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: James Sawalla Guseh, Larry A Allen, Silvia Castelletti et al.
articles.abstract: Athletes with myocarditis, pericarditis, valvular heart disease, and other acquired cardiovascular conditions require careful evaluation when considering competitive sports participation. This document outlines key clinical considerations, risk factors, and expert consensus, serving as the rationale for Section V of the recent AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities. Disease-specific risk stratification and shared decision-making are essential in determining return-to-play eligibility. This Task Force document addresses myocarditis, pericarditis, the cardiovascular impact of respiratory viral infections, incidental myocardial fibrosis, Kawasaki disease, infiltrative cardiomyopathies, and valvular heart disease.

articles.title: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome combined with obesity induces lipopolysaccharide cross-tolerance: A multi-cohort translational study.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Frank González, Robert V Considine, Ola A Abdelhadi et al.
articles.abstract: Women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) and obesity have significant chronic proinflammatory stress impacting metabolic health. We determined the effect of in vitro lipid exposure with and without lipopolysaccharide (LPS) on mononuclear cell (MNC)-derived inflammation in PMOS. Nineteen reproductive-age women with PMOS (10 lean, 9 with obesity) and 18 ovulatory controls (9 lean, 9 with obesity) participated in the study. Nuclear factor-κB (NFκB) activation and p50 subunit-precursor mRNA, toll-like receptor-4 (TLR-4) mRNA and protein, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFα) mRNA and secretion were quantified in cultured MNC exposed to lipid with and without LPS. Insulin sensitivity was determined during an oral glucose tolerance test (ISOGTT). Androgen secretion was assessed from blood collected before and 24, 48 and 72 hours after human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) administration. When LPS was absent, lipid-induced increases occurred in inflammation markers from MNC of both PMOS groups. When LPS was present, inflammation markers persistently increased from MNC of lean women with PMOS but decreased in those of women with PMOS and obesity concomitant with increases in p50-precursor mRNA and intranuclear anti-p50-bound NFκB indicating greater NFκB homodimer nuclear translocation. Both PMOS groups demonstrated decreased ISOGTT and higher HCG-stimulated androgen secretion compared with controls. When LPS was present, lipid-exposed inflammation responses negatively correlated with measures of adiposity and positively correlated with ISOGTT in PMOS. Women with PMOS and obesity demonstrate hallmark evidence of suppressed inflammation due to LPS cross-tolerance potentially providing a safeguard against worsening metabolic health instigated by the combined inflammatory load of PMOS and obesity.

articles.title: Targeting in vitro human white adipocyte metabolism with exercise mimicry - current insights and future directions.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Juulia H Lautaoja-Kivipelto, David Walzik, Philipp Zimmer et al.
articles.abstract: During the past decade, in vitro exercise mimicry has become a popular approach to examine intercellular communication and the effects of exercise-like stimulation and exerkines on various cell types, including white adipocytes. Despite the growing body of literature, a comprehensive overview of how human white adipocytes in vitro adapt to these approaches is lacking. In this review, we discuss the metabolic and functional effects of exercise mimicry on in vitro human white adipocytes. We compare the in vitro observations to in vivo findings to provide the reader with an up-to-date overview of the extent to which the responses of in vitro human white adipocytes to afore-mentioned treatments resemble human white adipose tissue (WAT) adaptations to exercise and exerkines. Finally, we discuss the limitations of the existing in vitro models and obtained results before providing suggestions for improved study designs in future experiments.

articles.title: Erratum. Multidimensional Comparison of Specific Strength Qualities Between Professional and Academy Rugby Union Players.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance

articles.title: Mental Fatigue Impairs Training Performance in Resistance-Trained Males and Females: A Velocity-Based Approach.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Emanuele Dello Stritto, Antonio Gramazio, Ruggero Romagnoli et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of mental fatigue (MF) on training volume and velocity of the first repetition during back squat in males and females. METHODS: Nineteen resistance-trained participants (10 males, 9 females) completed 6 training sessions. Four sessions served as familiarization with maximal intent velocity during the concentric phase and with different velocity loss (VL) thresholds. In the final 2 sessions, conducted in a randomized order, participants performed 8 back squat sets. The first 4 sets were completed under rested conditions, while the subsequent 4 sets were performed following either a 45-minute AX Continuous Performance Test test (MF condition) or a 45-minute documentary (control condition). The squat protocol involved 2 VL conditions (20% VL and 40% VL) and 2 loading intensities (60% and 80% 1-repetition maximum). Training volume was defined as the sum of repetitions across the 4 back squat sets. RESULTS: For training volume, a time × condition interaction emerged, indicating significant reductions in training volume in the MF condition in both sexes (P < .05, η2 = .39, -4.5 [4.6] repetitions in males and 9.11 [7.5] in females), whereas no significant changes were observed in the control condition (P > .05). Regarding velocity of the first repetition, a significant time × condition (P < .05, η2 = .26) and time × sex × condition interaction was found (P < .05, η2 = .06), showing a significant reduction in velocity of the first repetition only in the MF condition only, in both males (-0.06 [0.07] m/s) and females (-0.03 [0.05] m/s), with males exhibiting a greater decrease in velocity compared with females. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that resistance training performance may be negatively affected in the presence of MF, with this effect potentially differing between sexes.

articles.title: Exogenous Lactate Supplementation: A Promising Fueling Strategy to Enhance Endurance Performance.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Aitor Viribay, Adrián Castillo-García, Borja Martinez-Tellez
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Lactate has historically been mischaracterized as a metabolic byproduct associated with fatigue. The lactate shuttle paradigm describes its role in substrate exchange between glycolytic and oxidative tissues. Recent evidence has highlighted lactate as a key regulator of systemic energy metabolism and cellular signaling. While endogenous lactate production and clearance mechanisms during exercise are well established, the potential of exogenous lactate as an ergogenic fuel remains largely unexplored. Here, we aim to (1) synthesize current knowledge and discuss the mechanistic pathways through which exogenous lactate supplementation may enhance endurance performance in humans and (2) critically appraise the current limitations of high-dose exogenous lactate administration and outline novel formulation strategies, adapted from established sports nutrition practices, that warrant future investigation. CONCLUSION: Exogenous lactate supplementation holds promise as a novel fueling strategy to enhance endurance performance. However, human trials to date have failed to demonstrate performance benefits, potentially due to the low doses and bolus administration strategies employed. Future research should therefore focus on developing formulations capable of safely delivering physiologically relevant doses and evaluating their efficacy in well-controlled human studies.

articles.title: Longitudinal associations of anemia and iron status on early learning and memory: Evidence from eye-tracking assessments.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Davrina Rianda, Lisa M Oakes, Charles D Arnold et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anemia and iron deficiency (ID) remain prevalent among young children and may influence cognitive domains. OBJECTIVE: We examined associations of anemia and iron status at 6-9 months with attention, memory, and social visual engagement six months later using eye-tracking. METHODS: We analyzed cohort data from a randomized egg provision trial in rural Mangochi District, Malawi (n=660). In a subgroup (n=406), baseline biomarkers were measured, including hemoglobin, plasma ferritin, soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR), and body iron index (BII). Children were categorized as anemic (hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL), ID (ferritin <12 μg/L, sTfR >8.3 mg/L, or BII <0 mg/kg), and iron deficient anemic (IDA). At 12-15 months, attention was assessed using eye-tracking-based Infant Orienting with Attention task; recognition memory and social visual engagement were assessed using Visual Paired Comparison. Associations were evaluated using mixed-effect models adjusted for child, parental, and household characteristics. RESULTS: Among 406 children, 185 (45.6%) had anemia at baseline. Of 366 with iron data, 308 (84.2%) had ID, including 150 with IDA. Hemoglobin was associated with social visual engagement, and iron-specific biomarkers with memory. Per interquartile range (IQR) increase in hemoglobin, eyes dwell time decreased by 4% (95%CI -6%, -1%), mouth dwell time increased by 2% (95%CI 0%, 6%), and eye-mouth index decreased by 0.04 (95%CI -0.08, 0.00). IQR increases in ferritin, sTfR, and BII were associated with higher novelty preference (0.02; 95%CI 0.00, 0.02), lower peak look duration (-9.5%; 95%CI -14.8%, -2.9%), and lower shift rate (-0.02 shifts/s; 95%CI -0.04, 0.00), respectively. In multiplicity-corrected sensitivity analyses, only the sTfR-peak look duration association remained significant. Categorical anemia, ID, and IDA were not associated with outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Exploratory findings suggest that hemoglobin at 6-9 months was associated with social visual engagement, and iron-specific biomarkers with memory. Small effect sizes indicate modest longitudinal associations in this high-burden setting. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRY NUMBER: NCT03385252 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03385252).

articles.title: Extracellular matrix inhibits amino acid absorption mediated by Lactobacillus reuteri LR1 in ETEC-infected piglets.
articles.authors: Qingsong Tang, Yiyi He, Zhangjian Feng et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Small-intestinal mucosal architecture may affect amino acid (AA) absorption in weaned piglets. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate whether Lactobacillus reuteri (L. reuteri) LR1 improves small-intestinal AA absorption in enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) K88-challenged piglets and whether intestinal mucosal extracellular matrix (ECM) changes contribute. METHODS: Seventy-two 21-d-old weaned piglets were randomly assigned to 3 treatments (6 pens/treatment; 4 pigs/pen; 2 males/2 females). Control (CON) and ETEC K88 (K88) groups received a basal diet; the KLR group received basal diet plus 5 × 1010 CFU/kg L. reuteri LR1 for 14 days. K88 and KLR pigs received 5×1010 CFU of ETEC K88 by oral gavage on days 5, 7, and 9. Decellularized ECM (dECM) was isolated from piglet small intestine and tested for AA transport by Transwell assay. One pig per replicate (six/group) was sampled for analyses; three pigs/group were used for Transwell assays. Portal vein metabolites, liver free AAs, small-intestinal AA transporter and ECM-related gene expression, ECM protein, and dECM structure/transport were evaluated. Data were analyzed by unpaired two-tailed Student's t-test. RESULTS: K88 decreased the AA levels (L-glutamate, L-alanine, L-leucine, etc ) (36.3% to 51.2%), whereas KLR increased the AA levels (L-glutamate, L-aspartate, L-isoleucine, etc) in the portal vein of weaned piglets (134.6% to 179.3%, p < 0.05). K88 increased ECM-related genes (COL1A2, COL3A1, COL5A1, etc) (160.3% to 228.6%) expression and ECM deposition (136.4%) in the intestinal mucosa, whereas KLR reduced ECM-related genes (COL3A1, COL4A2, COL5A1, etc) (36.8% to 66.1%) expression and deposition (83.0%) in the intestinal mucosa (p < 0.05). Intestinal dECM showed a three-dimensional matrix network. Reducing the dECM content increased AA passage (148.3% to 226.5%, p < 0.05). dECM in the KLR reversed K88-induced reduction in AA absorption (K88 vs CON: 48.1% to 89.7%; KLR vs K88: 135.0% to 185.7%, p < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Dietary L. reuteri LR1 attenuated ETEC K88-induced impairment of small-intestinal AA absorption in weaned piglets, associated with reduced intestinal mucosal ECM deposition.

articles.title: Beyond glycemic index: Mixed meal postprandial glycemic response as a promising approach for Personalized Nutrition in Diabetes.
articles.authors: Shikha Nayar, S V Madhu
articles.abstract: Devising an effective tool for management of diet for patients with diabetes for a proper glycemic control has always been challenging due to the variability in available macronutrient content and composition of the meals along with the different factors affecting it. Traditionally, the concepts like glycemic index (GI) of food items, carbohydrate counting using the carbohydrate exchange lists have been largely guiding their food choices. These instruments, though useful, face certain paramount limitations that is, they are not mixed meal- based, intake responsive and sensitive to variations in the meal-composition, all of which is typical of different diets. The present perspective critically evaluates these and other associated issues considering supportive evidence available in this regard focusing on why mixed meal based glycemic responses are more pertinent for advising patients with diabetes. We also propose the need for developing a mixed meal- macronutrient exchange lists based on available macronutrients for patients with diabetes precisely characterizing the PPGR (post-prandial glycemic response) to different combination mixed meals in traditional diets. Furthermore, we suggest that the traditionally consumed mixed meals should be tested in different populations using continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) as an advance tool addressing the variability and possible combinations in traditional diets to obtain PPGR data sets. These then can be used for advising medical nutrition therapy for patients with diabetes recommending them with different traditional mixed meal combinations of their choice that keep their blood glucose in control.

articles.title: Low-Fat by Formulation, Not by Benefit: A Purified Low-Fat Diet Is Associated with Gut-Liver-Kidney Alterations in Rats.
articles.authors: Pedro Vieira, Gonçalo Ferreira, Filipa Carvalho et al.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: "Low-fat" claims are defined by a fat threshold, with no requirements regarding the nutrients replacing fat. Reformulation often relies on refined starches and free sugars at the expense of dietary fiber. Thus, a low-fat (LF) product is not necessarily of good carbohydrate quality, a dimension that macronutrient-based classification fails to capture. Whether LF-derived poor carbohydrate quality is associated with organ-specific alterations across the gut-liver-kidney axis remains unknown. Methods: Male Wistar rats were fed for 24 weeks a purified LF diet, its ingredient-matched purified high-fat, high-sucrose counterpart (HF), or a whole-grain Chow reference of similar energy density. Carbohydrate quality was assessed using the carbohydrate-to-dietary fiber-to-free sugars ratio. Body weight and adiposity, glucose homeostasis, gut fermentation, and hepatic and renal functional and structural parameters were evaluated. Results: Only Chow met the 10:1:1 carbohydrate quality criterion. At a caloric intake that did not exceed that of Chow, LF feeding was associated with increased body weight, adipocyte hypertrophy, impaired glucose tolerance and postprandial hyperinsulinemia. Fecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and branched SCFAs declined, consistent with a reduction in colonic fermentative output. Chronic LF exposure was additionally associated with hepatic and renal lipid accumulation, normoglycemic glycosuria, and podocyte structural alterations. Conclusions: A purified low-fat diet was associated with the same spectrum of gut, liver and kidney alterations as its high-fat counterpart, without excess caloric intake. These findings support an important role for nutrient sources and carbohydrate quality in shaping metabolic health beyond dietary fat content or caloric load alone.

articles.title: Effects of Omega-3 Supplementation on Inflammatory Biomarkers and Ambulatory and Central Blood Pressure in Patients Treated for Hypertension and Dyslipidemia: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Carol Kotliar, Rocío Martínez Vivot, Cristian Beltramo et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Omega-3 fatty acids exert anti-inflammatory and hemodynamic effects; however, their concurrent effects in patients receiving treatment for hypertension and dyslipidemia remain incompletely characterized. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of 12 weeks of supplementation with pharmaceutical-grade omega-3 fatty acids on inflammatory biomarkers, central and brachial blood pressure including office and 24 h ambulatory measurements, and vascular function in this population. METHODS: In this exploratory, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial, 100 adults received omega-3 ethyl esters at a capsule dose of 2 g/day or a matching placebo for 12 weeks, in addition to stable usual pharmacological treatment. Treatment effects were estimated using linear mixed-effects models. p-values were nominal, and 95% confidence intervals were not adjusted for multiplicity. RESULTS: Compared with placebo, omega-3 supplementation was associated with greater reductions in the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR; -0.43; 95% CI, -0.73 to -0.13; p = 0.005), ferritin (-47.32 ng/mL; 95% CI, -77.55 to -17.08; p = 0.003), daytime systolic blood pressure (-6.52 mmHg; 95% CI, -10.66 to -2.39; p = 0.002), nighttime diastolic blood pressure (-5.55 mmHg; 95% CI, -9.87 to -1.22; p = 0.013), central systolic blood pressure (-6.71 mmHg; 95% CI, -12.22 to -1.20; p = 0.019), and estimated pulse wave velocity (-0.77 m/s; 95% CI, -1.19 to -0.36; p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: The trial identified exploratory signals involving NLR, ferritin, selected ambulatory blood-pressure measures, central systolic blood pressure, and algorithm-derived ePWV. Multiplicity, limited sample size, and incomplete outcome availability preclude confirmatory interpretation. Independent replication in larger, prospectively registered trials with clearly specified endpoints and reproducible sample-size calculations is required.

articles.title: Macronutrient Intake and Clinical Manifestations in Adults with Long COVID-19: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of the BioICOPER Study.
articles.authors: David Rodríguez-García, Marta Gómez-Sánchez, Elena Navarro-Matías et al.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: The relationship between macronutrient intake and the clinical manifestations of long COVID-19 remains poorly understood. This study examined these associations in adults from the BioICOPER cohort. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 290 adults with long COVID-19 from the BioICOPER cohort who had complete seven-day dietary records collected using the EVIDENT application. Twelve clinical outcomes were assessed using linear regression with robust standard errors, ordinal logistic regression for frailty, and multinomial logistic regression for dyspnea. Model 1 examined eight exposures (total energy and seven nutrient intake variables), adjusting for age and sex. Model 2 examined seven exposures expressed as energy percentages or fiber density, additionally adjusting for total energy intake. Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied separately to the 96 and 84 tests, respectively. Results: In Model 1, higher intakes of total fat (odds ratio [OR]: 0.983; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.974-0.992), saturated fatty acids (OR: 0.956; 95% CI: 0.932-0.981), and monounsaturated fatty acids (OR: 0.967; 95% CI: 0.948-0.987), per additional g/day, were associated with lower odds of being in a higher frailty category (q: 0.034, 0.034, and 0.038, respectively). No primary association in Model 2 remained significant after correction for multiple testing. Exploratory analyses identified quadratic relationships between the energy percentages from protein and polyunsaturated fatty acids and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores (q = 0.0163 and 0.0111, respectively). Conclusions: Absolute intakes of certain fats were inversely associated with frailty, whereas the primary analyses of energy-adjusted dietary composition showed no significant associations after correction for multiple testing. These findings do not support recommending a specific macronutrient distribution. The exploratory cognitive findings require replication in longitudinal studies.

articles.title: Chemical Characterization and Effects of Aqueous Uncaria tomentosa Stem-Bark Extract on Keratinocyte Scratch Closure and Inflammatory and Redox Responses.
articles.authors: Euler Ribeiro-Filho, Verônica Farina Azzolin, Vitória Farina Azzolin et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Plant-derived bioactive compounds are increasingly investigated as modulators of cellular processes associated with healthy aging. Uncaria tomentosa is traditionally consumed as a botanical preparation, but the effects of its aqueous stem-bark extract on keratinocyte repair-related responses remain insufficiently characterized. METHODS: The extract was examined using colorimetric assays, DPPH radical scavenging, and untargeted LC-HRMS/MS with molecular networking and in silico class prediction. Cell viability, membrane integrity, extracellular NDUFS7, superoxide, nitric oxide-related products, and cell-cycle distribution were assessed at 1-100 µg/mL. Scratch closure, cytomorphology, IL-1β, and TNF-α were evaluated at 1, 3, and 10 µg/mL. RESULTS: The aqueous extract contained phenolic compounds, flavonoids, tannins, and alkaloids and exhibited DPPH-scavenging activity. LC-HRMS/MS supported a diverse profile including flavonoid glycosides, caffeoylquinic acids, procyanidins, iridoids, and putative triterpenoid glycosides. The extract preserved viability and membrane integrity and did not produce marked basal redox imbalance or increased extracellular NDUFS7. It moderately redistributed cell-cycle phases without a classical arrest pattern. Scratch closure increased at 6 and 24 h. IL-1β decreased at 1 and 3 µg/mL, whereas TNF-α remained broadly stable. CONCLUSIONS: The aqueous extract enhanced keratinocyte monolayer closure and selectively modulated inflammatory and redox-metabolic responses relevant to inflammaging. Cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype were not directly demonstrated.

articles.title: The Bioactive Potential of Algae and Their Health-Promoting Properties in the Context of the Impact on Human Health and Potential Applications in Food Technology: A Comprehensive Review.
articles.authors: Aleksandra Purkiewicz, Renata Pietrzak-Fiećko
articles.abstract: Algae are a promising source of biologically active compounds with potential significance for human health and modern food technology. Their diverse chemical composition includes, among other things, proteins and peptides, polyunsaturated fatty acids, polysaccharides, carotenoids, chlorophylls, polyphenols, vitamins, and minerals. The aim of this review is to provide a comprehensive characterization of the bioactive potential of algae and to analyze their health-promoting properties and potential applications in the production of functional foods. Particular attention was paid to compounds that have been shown in studies to exhibit antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antihypertensive effects, as well as those that potentially support normal glucose metabolism and have anticancer properties. The importance of selected algal components in protecting cells from oxidative stress and modulating metabolic processes was also discussed. From a food technology perspective, the possibilities for using algal biomass and components isolated from it as functional additives, natural colorants, texturizers, and sources of nutrients were presented. The potential of algae as an alternative source of protein and lipids in response to the growing demand for sustainable food raw materials was also considered. At the same time, limitations related to the bioavailability of bioactive compounds, variability in chemical composition, the presence of potential contaminants, and the need to standardize methods were highlighted. An analysis of the available data indicates that algae may be a valuable raw material for the development of functional foods; however, fully realizing their potential requires further in vivo studies and clinical trials to confirm their efficacy and safety.

articles.title: The Association of Type 2 Diabetes and Hypothyroidism with the Composition and Antioxidant Properties of Human Milk: A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.authors: Agnieszka Dombrowska-Pali, Agnieszka Chrustek, Dorota Olszewska-Słonina et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Thyroid disorders and diabetes are among the most common endocrine and metabolic conditions affecting pregnant women. It is important to note that adequate serum thyroid hormone levels are essential for proper lactation. Diabetes, in turn, is associated with delayed lactogenesis, especially in cases of poor glycemic control. It should be emphasized that breastfeeding is globally recognized as the safest and most effective method of feeding infants. Human milk has a variable nutritional composition in distinct phases: colostrum, transitional milk, and mature milk. METHODS: The present observational cross-sectional study included 208 breastfeeding women between 3 and 12 months postpartum: 79 women with hypothyroidism, 53 women with type 2 diabetes, and 76 healthy controls. An analysis was conducted on a sample of human milk to determine its basic nutritional composition, cortisol concentration, and antioxidant status. This analysis utilized DPPH and FRAP assays, which are methods employed to assess the antioxidant capacity of a sample. The basic composition of human milk was analyzed using the MIRIS HMATM analyzer (Uppsala, Sweden). Cortisol levels were determined using an immunoenzymatic method. RESULTS: In unadjusted analyses, milk fat content was higher in women with hypothyroidism and lower in women with type 2 diabetes compared with the control group. However, these differences were no longer statistically significant after adjustment for maternal and clinical covariates in multiple regression analyses. A lower reduction in the DPPH radical was shown in the milk of women with type 2 diabetes (13.8%) and in the milk of women with hypothyroidism (29%) compared to the control group. In the group of women with type 2 diabetes, cortisol levels positively correlated with the protein content and caloric content of milk. It was also noted that BMI in this group was significantly associated with the caloric content of human milk. CONCLUSIONS: These findings demonstrate differences in selected characteristics of human milk among the studied groups; however, their clinical relevance for infant health cannot be determined from the present study, as infant growth, body composition, and developmental outcomes were not assessed. Further prospective studies incorporating infant outcomes are needed to determine the clinical significance of these observations.

articles.title: Dietary Restriction Status for Hen's Egg, Cow's Milk, and Wheat in Relation to Plasma Amino Acid Profiles, Growth, and Insulin-like Growth Factor I in Children with Food Allergy.
articles.authors: Seiya Masukane, Suguru Fujita, Ayano Ueda et al.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Food avoidance may compromise nutrient intake and growth in children with food allergy; however, its association with plasma amino acid profiles remains poorly understood. We aimed to examine dietary restriction status for hen's egg, cow's milk, and wheat in relation to plasma amino acids, growth, and insulin-like growth factor I. Methods: This single-center cross-sectional study included 80 children aged < 10 years. Dietary restriction status, defined based on the amount of each food medically permitted for routine daily consumption, was dichotomized as complete avoidance/minimal intake or partial/unrestricted intake. Plasma amino acids were available for 79 participants. Multivariable models included all three foods, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Results: No broad reduction in plasma amino acid concentrations was evident across dietary restriction categories, although several food-specific associations were observed. Less restrictive cow's milk status was nominally associated with higher height standard deviation score (SDS) and lower aspartic acid concentration. Less restrictive wheat status was associated with lower weight SDS after multiple-testing correction (q = 0.046), although the complete avoidance/minimal intake group comprised only three participants. Among children with a cow's milk allergy, threonine concentration was 34.2% lower in the partial/unrestricted group than in the complete avoidance/minimal intake group (q = 0.002). The minimum essential amino acid z-score was inversely associated with weight SDS and body mass index SDS (q = 0.023 for both). No association with the overall 20-amino-acid profile remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Conclusions: Dietary restriction status was not accompanied by a broad or uniform reduction in circulating amino acids. Instead, the observed pattern suggested selective rather than generalized differences, warranting confirmation in longitudinal studies with quantitative dietary assessments.

articles.title: Associations of Anthropometry and Handgrip Strength with Bioelectrical Impedance Parameters in Irritable Bowel Syndrome: A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.authors: Jiří Vejmelka, Martina Kollerová, Ivana Pražanová et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Simple anthropometry may complement nutritional assessment in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). We examined the associations of arm anthropometry and handgrip strength (HGS) with bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) parameters. METHODS: This cross-sectional baseline analysis included 55 adults with IBS-D or IBS-M for valid non-adiposity measurements; 54 contributed valid paired body-fat estimates, and 54 had valid dominant-hand HGS. RESULTS: MUAMC correlated with BIA-derived skeletal muscle mass within men (Spearman's ρ = 0.748) and women (ρ = 0.673). After adjustment for sex, age, height and body weight, the MUAMC association was attenuated (β = 0.0337 kg/mm, 95% CI 0.0059-0.0616; p = 0.0187). MUAMC was correlated with phase angle in the pooled sample (ρ = 0.806), but sex-related differences were exploratory. In a sensitivity model using the impedance index, the association was not significant after further adjustment for body weight (β = 0.0670, 95% CI -0.0087 to 0.1427; p = 0.0816). HGS correlated with BIA-derived skeletal muscle mass before adjustment (ρ = 0.769; n = 54), whereas an adjusted association was not established. BIA- and skinfold-derived body-fat estimates were correlated but showed proportional bias, limiting interchangeability. CONCLUSIONS: MUAMC is associated with BIA-derived muscle-related parameters, but mathematical coupling, body size and the absence of a criterion method limit causal and validation claims. Findings from this exploratory single-centre analysis require independent confirmation.

articles.title: Mushrooms and Human Nutrition: Is It Time for a New Food Group?
articles.authors: Lora Iannotti, Gifty Aboagye-Mensah, Laura Brugger et al.
articles.abstract: In this narrative review, evidence is analyzed to help determine whether mushrooms should be recommended as a separate food group, based on 3 lines of inquiry: biochemistry, epidemiology, and sustainability. Mushrooms are classified taxonomically in the kingdom Fungi, distinct from Plantae or Animalia where most other foods are found. Yet around the world, food-based dietary guidelines group mushrooms with vegetables. We reviewed evidence from multiple databases and applied varying keyword strings for each area of inquiry, including (1) biochemistry, (2) epidemiology, and (3) sustainability. Studies published in English from 1990 to the present were included. Evidence from biochemistry showed mushrooms contain constituents-including ergothioneine, lectin, β-glucan, conjugated linoleic acid, micronutrients (vitamin D, niacin, choline, selenium, zinc), and other bioactive factors (phenolic compounds, terpenes)-linked to positive health outcomes with the potential to fill gaps left by other food groups. Experimental trials on human health effects are lacking, though observational studies of moderate quality showed mushroom consumption was associated with positive metabolic and neurocognitive outcomes. Regarding environmental sustainability, mushroom production on lignocellulose substrates requires minimal inputs, and spent substrate may be recycled into animal feed and biofuel, among other uses. Recommending mushrooms as a distinct group could relieve environmental pressure from other food groups. Social sustainability varies by region, with higher acceptability in Asia, cultural barriers evident in Europe and North America, and increasing consumption in South America. Economically, mushrooms show promise for revenue generation and affordability, despite sparse data and production limited to 5 mushroom types. Convincing rationale was found on the biochemistry and sustainability aspects of mushrooms to justify recommending them as a separate food group, but more empirical evidence linking mushrooms to health outcomes is needed.
